Compare how Texas housing markets weathered the 2008 crisis

txhome.Rmd

This guide shows how to use txhome to answer one question:

Which Texas housing markets were hit hardest by the 2007-2010 downturn, and how quickly did they recover?

It is written for economics students studying how the 2008 financial crisis affected regional housing markets, and assumes no previous experience with the package. It covers how to install the package, launch and use the app, and interpret the results.

Install the package 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-chenulidias")

Launch the app 

library(txhome)
run_app()

Use the app

The sidebar has three controls:

  1. Choose market areas: pick one or more of Texas’s 46 market areas. A market area is a local housing market, usually a city or county.
  2. Choose a measure: homes sold (the average number sold each month), the median sale price adjusted for inflation (in July 2015 dollars), or the median sale price as reported at the time.
  3. Compare areas as a percentage of their pre-crisis peak: rescales every area so its highest yearly level from 2000 to 2006 equals 100. This lets you compare large and small markets on the same chart.

The app then shows:

  • Two headline boxes: the chosen area that was hit hardest and the one that recovered fastest.
  • Over time: each chosen area from 2000 to 2015, with the 2007-2010 downturn shaded.
  • Summary table: each area’s pre-crisis peak, downturn low, percentage fall, and the year it got back to its peak.
  • All areas ranked: how far every Texas market fell, with your chosen areas highlighted.

If no areas are chosen, the app asks you to choose one. Kerrville and South Padre Island have no data before 2007, so the app explains that their fall and recovery can’t be measured.

Interpret the outputs

The app’s figures come from the package’s crisis_recovery() function, which you can also use directly. For each area, it finds:

  • the pre-crisis peak: the highest yearly level from 2000 to 2006;
  • the downturn low: the lowest yearly level from 2007 to 2010;
  • the change from peak to low, as a percentage; and
  • the recovery year: the first later year the area got back to its peak.

Each yearly level is the average of that year’s monthly values.

library(txhome)
crisis_recovery(measure = "sales", areas = c("Austin", "Dallas", "Houston")) |>
  dplyr::select(area, peak_year, peak, low_year, low, drop_pct,
                recovery_year, status) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Area", "Peak year", "Pre-crisis peak", "Low year",
                  "Downturn low", "Change (%)", "Back at peak in", "Status"),
    digits = 1
  )
Area Peak year Pre-crisis peak Low year Downturn low Change (%) Back at peak in Status
Austin 2006 2523.7 2010 1656.0 -34.4 2013 Recovered
Dallas 2006 5352.2 2010 3531.9 -34.0 - Not recovered by 2015
Houston 2006 6749.5 2010 4733.9 -29.9 2014 Recovered

Sales figures are average homes sold per month. Home sales in all three markets peaked in 2006 and were lowest in 2010, falling by roughly 30-35%. Their recoveries differed: Austin was back at its pre-crisis level by 2013, Houston by 2014, while Dallas had still not recovered when the data end in mid-2015.

A key finding: inflation hides real price falls

The app lets you switch between prices as reported and prices adjusted for inflation. This changes the answer to “did prices fall during the crisis?”. The table counts how many of the 46 areas fall into each outcome under each measure:

nominal <- crisis_recovery(measure = "median") |>
  dplyr::count(status, name = "Prices as reported")
real <- crisis_recovery(measure = "median_real") |>
  dplyr::count(status, name = "Adjusted for inflation")

dplyr::full_join(nominal, real, by = "status") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `Prices as reported` = dplyr::coalesce(`Prices as reported`, 0L),
    `Adjusted for inflation` = dplyr::coalesce(`Adjusted for inflation`, 0L)
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename(Outcome = status) |>
  knitr::kable()
Outcome Prices as reported Adjusted for inflation
Insufficient data 2 2
Never fell below peak 32 11
Recovered 12 25
Not recovered by 2015 0 8

Using prices as reported, most areas never fell below their pre-crisis peak. After adjusting for inflation, most areas did fall, and several had not recovered by 2015. Because prices in general rise over time, a home’s price can look steady while its real value is falling.

Limitations

  • The data end in July 2015, so recoveries after that are not captured.
  • Market areas are MLS (multiple listing service) regions, not exact city boundaries.
  • Median prices depend on which homes sell, so they can change even if individual home values do not.
  • The inflation adjustment uses the CPI for the US South region, which includes Texas but is not specific to it.

Data sources

Housing data were collected by the TAMU Real Estate Center and are distributed in the ggplot2 package as ggplot2::txhousing. Inflation data are the US Bureau of Labor Statistics South region CPI, retrieved from FRED.
